title: Shared Divisor of the Extremes
statement:
You get an array nums of positive integers. Take its smallest and its largest value, and return the greatest integer that divides both of them.

The values in between do not take part.

examples.why: The extremes are 4 and 12, and 4 divides both. The 7 in the middle is ignored; including it would give 1.
Smallest 9, largest 30. Their common divisors are 1 and 3.
The smallest and largest are the same value, which divides itself.

hints: First reduce the array to the two numbers that matter.
Trying every divisor from min down to 1 works but can take a billion steps. Is there a faster way to find the greatest common divisor of two numbers?
Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b), and gcd(a, 0) = a. Each step at least halves the numbers within two rounds.

explain.intuition:
Two passes of thinking. First, only the minimum and maximum matter, so one scan finds them. Second, the greatest common divisor of two numbers comes from Euclid's algorithm: any number dividing both a and b also divides a mod b, so you can keep replacing the larger number with the remainder until one of them is 0.

The remainders shrink fast, so the loop runs O(log max) times. Trying every candidate divisor from the minimum downward can take as many steps as the minimum itself.
steps: While lo ≠ 0: set (hi, lo) = (lo, hi mod lo).
pitfalls: Taking the gcd of the whole array instead of only its two extremes.
Using Math.min(...nums) on a huge array in JavaScript. Spreading 100 000 arguments can overflow the call stack; a loop is safe.
Counting down from the minimum in steps of 1. With values near 10^9 and coprime extremes, that is a billion iterations.

solutions.title: Try divisors from the minimum down
solutions.idea: The answer is at most the minimum. Check each candidate d from the minimum downward and return the first that divides both extremes.

solutions.title: Min, max, then Euclid
solutions.idea: Find the extremes in one scan and apply Euclid's remainder loop to them.

followups: Return the gcd of the whole array instead. Can you stop early?
Why does Euclid's algorithm need only O(log max) steps?
